error_note: Glycosuria does occur in Dent disease as part of proximal tubulopathy, but it is an inconstant, nonspecific feature; low-molecular-weight proteinuria and hypercalciuria are the characteristic findings.
Hyponatremia (SIADH) is an occasional complication of any encephalitis and says nothing specific about Japanese encephalitis.
A Brucella agglutinin titer measures pathogen-specific antibody, not total immunoglobulin; a high titer reflects Brucella exposure and has no bearing on ALPS type 4.
This is a lactose tolerance test, where a glucose rise after the lactose dose is the normal response showing lactase activity; 'high' is not hyperglycemia in the diabetic sense.
Lactic acidemia is real in DECR deficiency, but a 15-minute lactate after an unspecified (XXX) challenge has no defined 'high', and elevated lactate is shared by hundreds of disorders.
A high 90-minute OGTT glucose shows impaired glucose tolerance, which is an occasional, nonspecific consequence of catecholamine excess and not a marker of pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma.
Gliadin IgA is an antigen-specific celiac serology, not total serum IgA; a high result does not show the hyper-IgA reported in this congenital neutropenia.

Hypoglycemia from hypopituitarism fits the syndrome, but a 9th specimen after an unspecified (XXX) challenge has no defined 'low' (it could be an insulin tolerance test), and hypoglycemia is shared by over 200 diseases.
A low mugwort-specific IgE is the normal non-sensitised state and is not an abnormal total immunoglobulin concentration; it has no relation to panniculitis with lipodystrophy.

Anti-GPIIb/IIIa antibodies can accompany the autoimmune thrombocytopenia seen in ALPS, but they are the general finding of immune thrombocytopenia and are not a diagnostic or characteristic test for ALPS 2A.
Hypoglycemia is a very rare, nonspecific feature of congenital syphilis, and a 45-minute value after an unspecified (XXX) challenge has no defined 'low' in any case.
Thrombocytopenia is at most a very rare (<5%) and probably incidental annotation for fibular hemimelia, a limb malformation, and it is carried by over 400 diseases.

Baseline ACTH is markedly raised in familial glucocorticoid deficiency, but this is a glucagon stimulation timepoint where an ACTH rise is the normal response, so 'high' needs stimulated criteria and is not how the disease is shown.

A high cortisol after corticotropin is the normal stimulated response and does not show hypercortisolism; Cushing syndrome is in any case a very rare feature confined to McCune-Albright-type fibrous dysplasia.
A low algae-specific IgE is a normal finding and not an abnormal immunoglobulin concentration; Sezary syndrome is if anything associated with raised total IgE.

ACTH deficiency does occur in combined pituitary hormone deficiency, but an ACTH drawn 1.5 hours into a glucose load is not a recognised test of corticotroph reserve and 'low' is not defined for it; the feature is also only occasional.

A single-frequency left-ear pure-tone threshold characterises hearing loss but cannot diagnose DFNB48 specifically, which needs molecular testing; one ear at one frequency also stands in for the whole audiogram.
Enzyme assay is the right diagnostic test, but the code is a LOINC Part (LP) rather than a test, and the expected result is recorded as 'present' when the diagnostic finding is deficient activity.
A low or absent echovirus 4 complement-fixation titer means no recent infection with that serotype; it is not hypogammaglobulinemia.

The HIGH bands are fine, but the ABOVE_TARGET band (>=6.0 mg/dL on urate-lowering therapy) is a treatment target, not a definition of hyperuricemia; a man at 6.5 mg/dL is above target yet not hyperuricemic.
The test measures LH in semen, whereas the phenotype is about circulating (serum or plasma) LH.
A single-frequency left-ear threshold documents severity of hearing loss but does not diagnose DFNB79, which is a molecular diagnosis; one frequency in one ear stands in for the whole audiogram.

Lp(a) is a causal risk factor for atherosclerotic disease in general; it is raised in only a minority of patients with peripheral arterial disease, so 'expected result: increased' overstates a risk marker.
A single-frequency left-ear threshold characterises the hearing loss but cannot attribute it to DFNA53, as the curator text itself says; one frequency in one ear stands in for the whole audiogram.
Alanine is always present in serum; the informative finding is an elevated level, a nonspecific marker of lactic acidemia in mitochondrial disease, so 'expected result: present' says nothing.

GOLD grades stage severity in someone already shown to have a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70; FEV1 percent predicted alone does not indicate COPD, and the GOLD 1 band (>=80%) covers every normal result.
The nomogram lines are time-dependent and the code carries no time since ingestion, so the 16-hour band (>=18.75 mcg/mL) would label ordinary therapeutic levels as toxic.

Hyperuricemia is a risk factor for gout, not gout itself (most hyperuricemic people never develop it, and urate can be normal during a flare); the above-target band also presupposes a patient already treated for gout.
A platelet count directly determines whether the count is abnormal; it is declared uninformative only because critical (panic) limits of 37-910 were used as the band in place of a reference interval.
The HIGH band starts at 5.6 mmol/L, the upper fasting limit, but this code does not specify fasting; a random or post-prandial glucose of 6-7 mmol/L is not hyperglycemia.

Underclaim: declaring every digoxin result uninformative is too strong, since a grossly raised level (or an undetectable one) bears on digitalis toxicity even without a recorded sampling time; only borderline values depend on timing.

The 18.5-25 band is the adult WHO range but is labelled 'all populations'; children need age- and sex-specific percentiles (and some Asian guidelines use lower cut-offs), so a value in this band does not rule out abnormal BMI for them.
A normal total count does not exclude an abnormal lymphocyte subset count, which falls under this term (the curator note concedes this), and the adult interval is unsuitable for young children.

The direction and term are right, but a lower limit of 4.7 pmol/L for adult men is roughly tenfold below the usual male lower limit (about 40 pmol/L, 10 pg/mL), suggesting a unit or transcription error, so most truly low results would be missed.
